scenario.name: AWS EKS Security, Unit 42 & MITRE — Amazon EKS aws-auth ConfigMap system:masters RBAC Audit
scenario.overview: Imagine an underground city subway metro station with tiled tunnel walls, glowing route maps, chrome fare turnstiles, ticket kiosks, and a gleaming metro train sliding along the platform. Down in the underground subway concourse, a rider taps a replayed magnetic metro fare card at the chrome turnstile bank during evening rush hour. In this real-world scenario, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the metro station agent's station, then approaches the metro card turnstile bank disguised as a regular visitor. The metro booth attendant’s fare-gate console flags a single card swiped at two distant stations within seconds and alerts transit security. In this scenario (T1078.004, AWS EKS Security, Unit 42 & MITRE, Amazon EKS aws-auth ConfigMap system:masters RBAC Audit), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: eKS STS Presigned Bearer Token, then patching kube-system/aws-auth mapUsers /, then cluster-Admin Secret Enumeration. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering EKS STS Presigned Bearer Token, then Patching kube-system/aws-auth mapUsers /, then Cluster-Admin Secret Enumeration, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection pivots on CloudTrail Event 200 correlated across the documented kill chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: EKS STS Presigned Bearer Token Authentication (k8s-aws-v1.<base64>)
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1078.004 - Cloud Accounts)
stages.description: Down in the underground subway concourse, a rider taps a replayed magnetic metro fare card at the chrome turnstile bank during evening rush hour. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the metro station agent's station while everyday visitors and the metro station agent go about their routine. An AWS IAM principal authenticates to the Amazon EKS API server by generating a presigned STS GetCallerIdentity URL encoded as a Bearer token (k8s-aws-v1.<base64>), which aws-iam-authenticator maps to Kubernetes groups via kube-system/aws-auth (logged in Linux Audit Event 200 with EksClusterAuth=aws-iam-authenticator , k8s-aws-v1 token, CallerIamArn=arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/eks-ci-deployer/build-01, TargetConfigMap=kube-system/aws-auth so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes aws eks get-token --cluster-name prod-eks-cluster (which executes a cloud control-plane API or CLI operation , aws eks get-token --cluster-name prod-eks-cluster against AWS CloudTrail, GCP Cloud Audit, or so that harvests cloud identity tokens, escalates IAM privileges, or exfiltrates cloud data , T1078.004 during "EKS STS Presigned Bearer Token Authentication , k8s-aws-v1.<base64>" without deploying traditional endpoint malware, captured in CloudTrail / Unified Audit Log telemetry). Next, the follow-up artifact kubectl get configmap aws-auth -n kube-system -o yaml runs (which executes a Kubernetes API request or container runtime command , kubectl get configmap aws-auth -n kube-system -o yaml configuring pod security con so that breaks out of container cgroup/namespace isolation , T1078.004 during "EKS STS Presigned Bearer Token Authentication , k8s-aws-v1.<base64>" to gain unrestricted root execution on the underlying Kubernetes worker node and access host credentials , kubelet / systemd). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ GET /api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/configmaps/aws-auth / ⇠#1 ACK 200) from Node ① (#1 Compromised CI/CD IAM Role) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 system:masters ClusterAdmin Access).

stages.title: Stage 2: Patching kube-system/aws-auth mapUsers / mapRoles with system:masters Group
stages.subtitle: Persistence & Privilege Escalation (T1098 - Account Manipulation)
stages.description: The turnstile arm clicks open, letting the rider step onto the platform and slip through the driver’s unlocked service door at the front of the subway car. Here in Step 2 inside the subway metro, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the underground subway train car without disturbing the emergency exit stairs. Using update/patch permissions on ConfigMaps in kube-system, the actor appends a secondary IAM role or user ARN into data.mapUsers with groups: ["system:masters"], granting persistent cluster-admin authority that bypasses Kubernetes RoleBindings (logged in Linux Audit Event 200 with AuditVerb=patch , kube-system/aws-auth, InjectedMapping=rolearn: readonly-audit-role -> groups: [system:masters], PrivilegeLevel=Built-in Kubernetes Superuser , system:masters so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes fields @timestamp, user.username, objectRef.name, requestObject.data.mapUsers | filter objectRef.name == "aws-auth" and verb in ["update", "patch"] (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , fields @timestamp, user.username, objectRef.name, requestObject.data.mapUsers | filter objec so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1098 during "Patching kube-system/aws-auth mapUsers / mapRoles with system:masters Group" , Using update/patch permissions on ConfigMaps in kube-system, the actor appends a secondary IAM role or user ARN into data while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact kubectl describe configmap aws-auth -n kube-system runs (which executes a Kubernetes API request or container runtime command , kubectl describe configmap aws-auth -n kube-system configuring pod security contex so that breaks out of container cgroup/namespace isolation , T1098 during "Patching kube-system/aws-auth mapUsers / mapRoles with system:masters Group" to gain unrestricted root execution on the underlying Kubernetes worker node and access host credentials , kubelet / systemd). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ PATCH /api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/configmaps/aws-auth (mapRoles -> system:masters) / ⇠#2 ACK 200) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Amazon EKS Control Plane API), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 system:masters ClusterAdmin Access).

keySpecs.value: fields @timestamp, user.username, objectRef.name, requestObject.data.mapUsers | filter objectRef.name == "aws-auth" and verb in ["update", "patch"]

stages.title: Stage 3: Cluster-Admin Secret Enumeration & EKS Access Entry Remediation
stages.subtitle: Credential Access (T1552.007 - Container API)
stages.description: Inside the subway cab, the intruder reads the station relay schedule and triggers an unauthorized express skip past the next inspection stop. In this final step inside the subway metro, the intruder approaches the metro card turnstile bank disguised as a regular visitor until the fare-gate audit console catches the mismatch. Authenticating as the newly mapped IAM role, the actor inherits system:masters group membership (which is hardcoded into kube-apiserver to bypass RBAC authorization checks) and lists cluster secrets (logged in Linux Audit Event 200 with EffectiveGroup=system:masters, AuthzDecision=allow , Built-in Superuser Group, TargetResource=/api/v1/secrets so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes aws eks update-cluster-config --name prod-eks-cluster --access-config authenticationMode=API (which executes a cloud control-plane API or CLI operation , aws eks update-cluster-config --name prod-eks-cluster --access-config authenticationMode=API so that harvests cloud identity tokens, escalates IAM privileges, or exfiltrates cloud data , T1552.007 during "Cluster-Admin Secret Enumeration & EKS Access Entry Remediation" without deploying traditional endpoint malware, captured in CloudTrail / Unified Audit Log telemetry). Next, the follow-up artifact aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name prod-eks-cluster runs (which executes a cloud control-plane API or CLI operation , aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name prod-eks-cluster against AWS CloudTrail, GCP Cloud so that harvests cloud identity tokens, escalates IAM privileges, or exfiltrates cloud data , T1552.007 during "Cluster-Admin Secret Enumeration & EKS Access Entry Remediation" without deploying traditional endpoint malware, captured in CloudTrail / Unified Audit Log telemetry). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ LIST /api/v1/secrets as group system:masters / ⇠#3 ACK 200) from Node ③ (#3 Amazon EKS Control Plane API) to Node ④ (#4 kube-system/aws-auth ConfigMap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 system:masters ClusterAdmin Access).

keySpecs.value: Switch the EKS cluster to authenticationMode=API (disabling the aws-auth ConfigMap completely) and audit all EKS Access Entries via AWS CloudTrail.
